notes:
BUILD: Copied all *.cpp/*.h + Makefile to scratchpad/audit-build, ran `make`. Build succeeded (exit 0) with 3 pre-existing -Wreturn-type warnings: SymbolTable.cpp:172 (SymbolTable::create_new_scope_table), Typechecker.cpp:243 (Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains), Typechecker.cpp:1211 (Typechecker::check_return_statement) - all three functions fall off their end without a return on some path (g++ note, no -Wall needed).

CRASH ROOT CAUSE (affects 6/14 shipped test programs: logicals.src, math.src, recursiveFib.src, test2.src, custom_math.src, math_fail.src - all exit 132/SIGILL): Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains @ Typechecker.cpp:203-243. The switch(previous_token_type) at lines 216-239 has cases T_ASSIGN/T_COLON/T_EXCLAM/T_GREATER/T_LESS that just `break;` with no return, and the function's final `return true;` is commented out (line 242: `//return true;`). Any two-char operator built by chaining single-char tokens (`<=`,`>=`,`==`,`!=`,`:=`) that matches one of those cases falls off the end of a non-void function -> UB -> g++ -g -O0 emits a trap instruction, observed as SIGILL. Confirmed via gdb: crash lands exactly at Typechecker.cpp:227 (`case T_EXCLAM: break;`), call chain parse_if_statement -> parse_expression -> parse_arithOp -> parse_relation -> Typechecker::feed_in_tokens (Typechecker.cpp:98) -> second_relation_token_chains. This matches a bug already flagged in the repo's own CLAUDE.md "Known broken state", so I am not reporting it as new, only independently reconfirming it (fresh gdb backtraces) and adding one new empirical detail: minimal repro shows `<=`/`==` crash inside an `if(...)` condition but the identical `<=` inside a `for(...)` condition does NOT crash (p1_for_le.src, exit 0) - root cause of that asymmetry not further chased (speculative:true) but the if-condition trigger is 100% reproducible across every probe/test file I tried.

All items below were independently confirmed via fresh reads + runnable minimal reproductions in scratchpad/probes/, not copied from CLAUDE.md.

NEW FINDING 1 - false "parsed successfully" banner when the only diagnostic is an if/loop-condition type error: parser.cpp:12-21 decides the "parsed successfully with no errors" vs "...with errors" banner purely from `errors_occured` (parser member), printed at parser.cpp:14-21, then `print_errors()` (parser.cpp:27) dumps the queued messages afterward. But Typechecker::check_if_statement (Typechecker.cpp:1213-1228), the function used for both if-conditions and for-loop conditions, only sets `type_error_occured` (a Typechecker-local flag, Typechecker.cpp:1223) and calls `generate_error_report` (Typechecker.cpp:1221) - it never sets `parser_parent->errors_occured = true`. The call sites in parser.cpp (parse_if_statement: parser.cpp:1650-1657; parse_loop_statement: parser.cpp:1806-1813; and a third at parser.cpp:1931-1937) only ever read/reset `type_checker->type_error_occured`, never propagate it into `errors_occured`. Net effect: every program whose only defect is an if/loop condition type mismatch prints "The program parsed successfully with no errors" immediately followed by the actual "Error on line N: ..." text - a directly self-contradicting summary line. Reproduced minimally with probes/p6_if_string.src (7 lines) and also seen in the shipped testPgms/correct/test1.src ("The program parsed successfully with no errors" then "Error on line 23: If statements must resolve..."). Verdict for these runs: wrong-output (contradictory success/error reporting), not merely a cosmetic nit since a caller/grader parsing only the summary line would be misled into believing the program is error-free.

NEW FINDING 2 - multi-parameter procedure declarations are structurally unparseable: parser::parse_parameter_list (parser.cpp:1197-1233) is recursive. On seeing a comma (parser.cpp:1209) it consumes the comma and recurses (parser.cpp:1211-1212); the recursive (inner) call itself checks for the closing T_RPARAM and consumes it (parser.cpp:1215-1219) before returning. Control then resumes in the outer/caller frame at parser.cpp:1215, which re-checks Current_parse_token_type == T_RPARAM - but that paren was already consumed by the inner frame, so Current_parse_token is now whatever follows the parameter list (e.g. the `variable` keyword of the procedure body). The outer frame's check therefore always fails, unconditionally emitting "Missing \")\" to close procedure parameter list" (parser.cpp:1227) for ANY procedure declared with 2+ parameters. Verified with probes/p4b_two_params_ok.src (`procedure addTwo : integer(variable x : integer, variable y : integer)`) - fails to parse even though it is syntactically and semantically valid. Confirmed via grep that no file in testPgms/{correct,custom,fail} declares a multi-parameter procedure, so this defect is completely untested by the shipped suite.

NEW FINDING 3 - multi-argument procedure calls are structurally broken (different bug from #2, same symptom class): parser::parse_argument_list (parser.cpp:2550-2567). On seeing a comma (parser.cpp:2560) it recurses immediately at parser.cpp:2562 WITHOUT first consuming the comma token (contrast with parse_parameter_list, which does call Get_Valid_Token() before recursing). The recursive parse_expression() call then starts parsing with Current_parse_token still sitting on the comma itself, which is not a valid factor start, producing a cascade of unrelated parser errors ("Invalid token for factor discovered", "Error in expression", "Missing required \")\" for the end of a procedure call"). Verified with probes/p4_wrong_argcount.src (calling a 1-param procedure with 2 args). Because of Finding 2, a "correct" 2-parameter call could not be isolated from the declaration-side bug, but the call-site comma-consumption bug is visible independently in the error text pattern and confirmed by reading the code (no Get_Valid_Token() between the comma check and the recursive call, parser.cpp:2560-2563).

NEW FINDING 4 - no detection of undeclared variables or undeclared procedures at all: grep across parser.cpp/Typechecker.cpp/SymbolTable.cpp/ScopeTable.cpp finds zero "undeclared"/"not declared"/"not found"/"unknown identifier" diagnostic strings anywhere in the codebase. parser::parse_name (parser.cpp:2502-2546) and the is_in_table guards used throughout (e.g. parser.cpp:1645-1649, 1801-1805, 1926-1930) only have a positive branch that updates context when an identifier IS found in the current scope table; there is no corresponding error branch when it is not found - the parser just proceeds with whatever stale/default token it already had. Empirically: (a) calling an entirely undeclared procedure (probes/p3_undeclared_proc.src, `a := doesNotExist(1);`) produces "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - zero diagnostics of any kind; (b) referencing a plain undeclared variable (probes/p2_undeclared_var.src, `a := b + 1;` with `b` never declared) does not get a "undeclared" message either - it silently gets typed as empty string and later trips a confusing generic message "Error on line 4: Type \"\" and type \"\" have no valid operations" instead of a clear "b is not declared" error. This goes beyond the CLAUDE.md note about procedure-call arity not being checked - there is no undeclared-identifier detection of any kind, for variables OR procedures.

NEW FINDING 5 (spec violation, confirmed against spec2023.txt) - no array bounds checking at all: spec2023.txt lines 161-165 state as a required semantic rule: "13. Array indexes must be of type integer. Bounds checking to insure that the index is within the upper and lower bound (always 0) is required for all indexed array references." Probe p8_array_bounds.src declares `variable arr : integer[5];` then writes `arr[10] := 2;` (a compile-time-constant out-of-bounds index) and gets "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - no bounds check of any kind exists in the code (grepped for "bound"/"index" related error strings, found none). This is a direct, confirmed spec violation, distinct from and not mentioned in the repo's CLAUDE.md known-bugs list.

NEW FINDING 6 (spec violation, confirmed) - assignment type compatibility rule not enforced for incompatible types: spec2023.txt lines 166-172, rule 14, states assignment target and expression "must, in general, be of the same type. However, (i) bool and integer types are compatible, and (ii) integer and float types are compatible." Probe p5b_string_to_int.src assigns a string literal directly to an integer variable (`a := \"hello\";`) and gets "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - clearly outside the two spec-permitted exceptions, yet accepted. (Consistent with CLAUDE.md's documented `check_assignment_statement` stub, but I obtained fresh, concrete empirical proof of a specific spec-violating case; not re-reporting the stub itself as new.) By contrast, probe p5a_float_to_int.src (`a := f;`, integer := float) also produced no error, but per spec rule 14(ii) that actually IS the correct/expected outcome (int/float are declared compatible), so p5a's "no error" is NOT a bug, only p5b (string->int) is.

NEW FINDING 7 - cross-procedure Typechecker state leak produces false-positive "If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer" errors on structurally valid for-loop conditions in a LATER, unrelated procedure: Minimal repro probes/p13_two_procs.src - procedure `if_proc` contains a normal `if(true) then ... else ...` statement; the textually later, unrelated procedure `for_proc` contains `for(i := 0; i < zach) ... end for;` where i and zach are both plain integers. Output: "The program parsed successfully with no errors" followed by "Error on line 16: If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer" attributed to a line inside the for-loop BODY (not even the condition). An isolated for-loop with the identical `i < zach` condition and no preceding if-statement (probes/p12b_loop_less.src) produces zero errors, proving the false positive is caused by residual/stale Typechecker state (first_token/second_token/relation_tokens or type_error_occured, per Typechecker.cpp instance members) leaking across statement/procedure boundaries from the earlier if-statement into the later for-loop's condition check. This exact pattern (spurious if-statement-worded error on a for-loop, off by one line) is also visible in the shipped testPgms/correct/test1.src and test1b.src, which both contain an if_proc followed by a for_proc and both get this same bogus error - meaning two of the professor-provided "correct" test programs are misdiagnosed as containing type errors that do not exist. (The reused "If statements must..." wording for loop conditions, and the off-by-one line-number attribution from `Lexer->current_line`, are separately already documented in CLAUDE.md; the NEW part is the cross-procedure state-leak causing an outright false positive on code that is valid by every rule in the spec.)

NEW FINDING 8 - `return <procedure_call>;` (returning the result of a call expression directly) triggers a false-positive return-type mismatch, even when both procedures' declared return types match exactly: Typechecker::check_return_statement (Typechecker.cpp:1172-1211) is invoked from parser::parse_return_statement (parser.cpp:1917-1941). Minimal repro probes/p11d_return_call.src: `procedure Inner : integer() begin return 1; end procedure; procedure Outer : integer() begin return Inner(); end procedure;` yields "Error on line 10: Procedure is of type \"\" which is not compatible with return type of \"Integer\"" even though Inner and Outer are both declared `: integer`. By contrast, `return 5;` (literal) and `return v;` (plain local variable) both work correctly in isolation (probes/p11_simple_return.src, p11b_return_var.src). The bug is isolated specifically to returning a procedure-call expression: parser.cpp:1926 looks up `expression_parse.resolved_token.stringValue` in the current scope's symbol table to re-resolve its declared type, but for a call expression the resolved token apparently does not carry a stringValue/type that resolves correctly, leaving `updated_token`'s type empty ("") and the compatibility check in check_return_statement fails. Grepped all of testPgms/{correct,custom,fail} for `return .*(` (a direct return of a call) and found zero matches, so this path is completely untested by the shipped suite.

NEW FINDING 9 (confirmed, high-severity spec violation, and matches task's scope-id-reuse probe) - a local variable belonging to one procedure is visible/resolvable from a completely unrelated sibling procedure with no error, violating spec2023.txt lines 115-125 (rule 3/4: variables declared without `global` are local to their declaring procedure and "not visible outside of that procedure"). Minimal clean repro probes/p9b_scope_reuse_clean.src: `Outer` contains a nested `Inner` procedure that declares local `variable innerVal : integer;`; after `Inner`'s scope closes, a later, textually-sibling procedure `Sibling` (declared as a sibling of Outer, not nested inside it) does `result := innerVal;` and the compiler reports "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - `innerVal` is silently resolved (or at least never flagged as undeclared) even though it should be out of scope. This is consistent with, and gives concrete new proof for, the scope-id-reuse mechanism CLAUDE.md flags abstractly ("scope ids are reused by later sibling procedures") - I'm reporting the concrete observable defect (cross-scope variable leakage with zero diagnostics), which CLAUDE.md does not itself claim as a proven consequence.

MINOR - stray unformatted debug output bypasses the error-reporting pipeline: parser::resync_parser's "start state" switch has a `default: std::cout << "Error in resync start state" << std::endl;` (parser.cpp:3040, and an identical second copy at parser.cpp:3282) that prints directly to stdout outside the generate_error_report/print_errors mechanism (no "Error on line N:" formatting, printed immediately rather than batched at the end). Reproduced with probes/p7_unterminated_comment.src (nested `/* /* */` where only the inner block is closed): output includes the raw "Error in resync start state" line ahead of the two properly-formatted error lines. Functionally the unterminated/malformed nested comment IS still caught correctly overall ("Unclosed block comment detected", no crash, no hang) - just with one out-of-band debug line polluting the output.

Not investigated further due to scope/time: the exact reason `<=` crashes inside `if(...)` but not inside `for(...)` (Finding/root-cause section above, marked speculative); why check_return_statement's stale-state guard (`type_error_occured`) doesn't also catch Finding 8's case; whether SymbolTable::create_new_scope_table's missing-return path (SymbolTable.cpp:172, the third -Wreturn-type warning) is reachable/harmful - not probed directly.
probe_findings:
All probes run from /tmp/claude-1000/-datadrive-data-compiler-course/e0905122-5395-4b36-add9-f6a81e41bd28/scratchpad/probes/ against the built ./compiler.

(1) <= then == crash isolation: probes/p1_le.src (`if(a <= b) then ...`) -> exit 132 SIGILL. probes/p1_eq.src (`if(a == b) then ...`) -> exit 132 SIGILL. Both crash identically inside Typechecker::second_relation_token_chains (Typechecker.cpp:227), confirmed via gdb. Interesting asymmetry: probes/p1_for_le.src, identical `<=` but inside a `for(...)` condition instead of `if(...)`, does NOT crash (exit 0, "parsed successfully with no errors") - behaves INCORRECTLY (crash) for if-conditions, correctly/no-crash for for-conditions with the same operator (root cause of the asymmetry not further chased).

(2) Undeclared variable use: probes/p2_undeclared_var.src (`a := b + 1;`, b never declared) -> exit 0, "parsed successfully with errors", but the message is a confusing generic "Error on line 4: Type \"\" and type \"\" have no valid operations" rather than an "undeclared identifier" error. Behaves incorrectly - wrong diagnostic, not a real "undeclared" check.

(3) Undeclared procedure call: probes/p3_undeclared_proc.src (`a := doesNotExist(1);`) -> exit 0, "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - ZERO diagnostics. Behaves incorrectly (missed-error, complete silence).

(4) Wrong argument count: probes/p4_wrong_argcount.src (1-param procedure called with 2 args) -> exit 0, "parsed successfully with errors" but with cascading generic parser errors ("Invalid token for factor discovered", "Error in expression", "Missing required \")\" ...") rather than a clean argument-count diagnostic; traced to a real parser bug (comma not consumed in parse_argument_list, parser.cpp:2560-2563). Separately, declaring ANY procedure with 2+ parameters is itself unparseable (probes/p4b_two_params_ok.src fails with "Missing \")\" to close procedure parameter list" even though syntactically valid) - a distinct parser.cpp:1197-1233 recursion bug. Behaves incorrectly on both the call side and the declaration side.

(5) float->int and string->int assignment: probes/p5a_float_to_int.src (`a := f;`, int := float) -> exit 0, no error - CORRECT per spec rule 14(ii) (int/float declared compatible), so this is expected/ok behavior. probes/p5b_string_to_int.src (`a := \"hello\";`, int := string) -> exit 0, no error - INCORRECT, spec rule 14 requires target/expression types match except for bool/int and int/float; string->int is not one of the exceptions and should be rejected but silently passes.

(6) if-condition of type string: probes/p6_if_string.src (`if(s) then ...` where s : string) -> exit 0 banner "parsed successfully with no errors" immediately followed by "Error on line 5: If statements must resolve to either type Bool or Integer". The rejection itself is CORRECT (string condition is properly flagged), but the surrounding "parsed successfully" banner is wrong/self-contradictory (parser.cpp's errors_occured flag never gets set by this code path) - partially correct, partially wrong-output.

(7) nested block comment left unterminated: probes/p7_unterminated_comment.src (`/* outer /* inner */` - only inner closed) -> exit 0, "The program had parsing errors", correctly reports "Error on line 3: Unclosed block comment detected" (plus one cascading "Expected keywords ... not found"). No crash, no hang - behaves correctly overall, except for one extra unformatted debug line "Error in resync start state" printed to stdout ahead of the real errors (parser.cpp:3040/3282), which is a minor output-format defect.

(8) array declared+indexed, out-of-bounds constant index: probes/p8_array_bounds.src (`variable arr : integer[5];` then `arr[10] := 2;`) -> exit 0, "parsed successfully with no errors" - NO bounds checking performed, despite spec2023.txt:161-165 explicitly requiring it ("Bounds checking to insure that the index is within the upper and lower bound ... is required for all indexed array references"). Behaves incorrectly (missed-error, confirmed spec violation).

(9) two sibling procedures after a nested one, second references first's local (scope-id reuse probe): probes/p9b_scope_reuse_clean.src - `Outer` nests `Inner` (which declares local `innerVal`); sibling procedure `Sibling` (declared after Outer, not nested in it) does `result := innerVal;` -> exit 0, "The program parsed successfully with no errors" - `innerVal` is NOT flagged as out-of-scope/undeclared, i.e. it is effectively resolved or at least silently tolerated across an illegal scope boundary. Behaves incorrectly per spec (rule 3/4: locals not visible outside their declaring procedure) - a real, previously-unconfirmed consequence of the documented scope-id-reuse mechanism. (A richer version of this probe, p9_scope_reuse.src, additionally surfaced an unrelated false-positive return-type bug - see Finding 8 above re `return Inner();` - which had to be isolated separately in p9b to get a clean read on the scoping question itself.)

(10) 'global' declared inside a procedure, referenced from another procedure: probes/p10_global_in_proc.src - `ProcA` declares `global variable sharedVal : integer;` inside its own body and assigns it; sibling `ProcB` reads `sharedVal` with no local declaration -> exit 0, "The program parsed successfully with no errors", sharedVal resolves correctly across both procedures. This matches spec2023.txt:118-122 ("Any variable or procedure with the global reserved word prefix is a member of the global scope (no matter where it is declared)") - CORRECT/expected behavior, not a bug.
